# Data, Knowledge, and Representation {#sec-data-representations-world-models}

![](images/ch04-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="A source-linked project record feeds a task-specific representation that exposes some properties while declaring blind spots and retaining provenance."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world."
>
> — Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* (1922) [@Wittgenstein1922Tractatus, sec. 5.6]
:::

Data is the fuel for machine learning. It supplies examples from which models learn, context that helps them propose useful changes, and feedback that reveals whether those changes work. In AI-native architecture design, these roles connect learning to the engineering work of generating hardware and software that can be implemented and evaluated together. Useful data must describe more than the appearance of a design. It must connect design choices to behavior, cost, and the conditions under which those consequences were observed.

This chapter develops how to make those connections. Starting from an architectural question, it examines the kinds of information needed, what existing sources provide, and what a study must collect for itself. Hardware data can be scarce even when code is plentiful because obtaining a useful observation requires the right workload, tools, and implementation context. Collection cost, coverage, and curation therefore shape what a learning method can accomplish.

Observations become reusable architectural knowledge when we can explain why a design behaved as it did and when that explanation still applies. Representations determine which relationships a computational method can use to predict outcomes, optimize choices, or generate new designs. The chapter examines these choices alongside the restrictions on using and sharing the resulting data, preparing the information needed for the life cycle in @sec-architecture-20-ontology.

## Data Requirements for AI-Native Design

An AI-native design system needs information for several different purposes. To propose a change, it needs the intended computation, the existing design, and the constraints on what may change. To predict the consequences, it needs observations that connect comparable choices to outcomes. To evaluate a proposal, it needs workloads, expected behavior, and a suitable model or implementation. To explain the result, it needs enough detail to distinguish why one alternative worked better than another. These uses can share sources, but they do not all require the same dataset.

The accumulator study in @sec-architecture-20-ontology asks whether a different neural processing unit (NPU) organization can improve throughput. Consider a related Lighthouse question: can a compiler schedule a perception computation to reduce data movement and execution time on a candidate NPU? This hypothetical study initially holds the hardware organization and required numerical behavior fixed while allowing changes to tiling and scheduling. The computation and its dependencies help define possible schedules; evaluations on the target connect those choices to correctness and performance. The example examines another part of the same system without assuming that the earlier block study has produced a working design.

The first data-design decision is what counts as an example. For a kernel-latency predictor, one evaluated sample might pair an operator and its input shape with a compiler schedule, a hardware configuration, and the measured latency. A collection of source kernels supplies possible inputs, but it does not supply their performance on the intended NPU. Producing those labels requires compilation, correctness checks, and evaluation. For a schedule generator, source kernels describe the computations to be scheduled. Examples of scheduling transformations would additionally need to connect those computations to the schedules that implement them. Correctness checks and performance measurements would show which transformations preserve the required behavior and when they help. We can judge a collection's usefulness only after identifying the task it is meant to support.

A *representation* gives selected properties a form that a computational method can use [@BengioEtAl2013RepresentationLearning]. A predictor might consume a compact description of a schedule; a generator needs a form in which it can express changes. The detailed choices come later in @sec-hardware-representation-formats. At this point, the distinction is between acquiring relevant information and choosing how a method will use it. Neither requires every project to train a new model from scratch. Existing models, retrieved material, and newly collected observations can contribute different parts.

The progression in @fig-architecture-data-progression connects those decisions. Specifications, register-transfer level (RTL) code, execution traces, and electronic design automation (EDA) reports provide artifacts and observations; a checked dataset organizes them for use; explanations capture what can be learned from them; and representations expose the properties a method needs. These connections also let us distinguish a proposed schedule from one that has been evaluated. The generated schedule describes a candidate; its linked checks and measurements show what is known about its behavior. If the compiler or hardware changes, those links help identify which observations may need to be collected again.

![**Architectural sources support different tasks through linked datasets, knowledge, and representations.** Raw source artifacts (specifications, RTL netlists, execution traces, EDA signoff logs) enter a checked dataset and separate into durable project knowledge versus live project state before feeding linked native, structured, or optional learned representations. Source identity, versions, acquisition conditions, and access limits remain attached throughout the handoff, ensuring derived views add analytical capabilities without displacing native artifacts as the source of record. Conceptual transformation pipeline.](images/fig-architecture-data-progression){#fig-architecture-data-progression width="100%" fig-alt="A left-to-right sequence begins with heterogeneous architecture sources, passes through a checked dataset, separates durable knowledge from current project state, and forms linked native, structured, and optional learned representations before method choice. A bar across the bottom states that source identity, versions, acquisition conditions, and links remain attached throughout. Native artifacts remain the source of record."}

The starting point is therefore an inventory of needed information, followed by an examination of the sources that can provide it. Access restrictions affect that inventory from the outset; their consequences for using and sharing data are developed in @sec-architecture-data-access.

## Heterogeneous Architectural Data Sources

Architectural information comes from descriptions of intended behavior, artifacts that implement it, observations of execution, and explanations of design choices. These sources span the software and hardware stack. A specification states what a system should do; source code and compiler artifacts describe how a computation is organized; a simulator or measurement reports what happened under particular conditions. Physical reports add implementation costs that a software trace cannot establish. Design review notes can explain why an alternative was chosen or ruled out, including constraints absent from automated tool outputs.

Each source answers part of the question. Collecting more of one kind cannot replace a missing connection to another. The main source families follow the computation from software to physical implementation:

- **Software and compiler artifacts.** Source programs describe the computation, while compiler intermediate representations (IRs) expose operations, dependencies, and implementation choices such as tiling and scheduling. Binaries identify the executable being evaluated; execution traces and profiles record its observed behavior. LLVM and Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) provide examples of intermediate representations, whose structure and uses are developed in @sec-hardware-representation-formats.
- **Simulation models and execution results.** Models describe selected aspects of the hardware, while their outputs report behavior under particular workloads and configurations. Depending on the model, useful observations can include execution cycles, memory transfers, contention, and queue occupancy. Tools such as gem5, SCALE-Sim, ChampSim, and Ramulator examine different parts of this behavior. The dataset needs to retain what each model represents and which effects it leaves out.
- **Implementation artifacts, checks, and measurements.** RTL and synthesized netlists describe hardware implementations. Testbenches, assertions, and verification results connect those implementations to required behavior. Synthesis and physical-design tools add area, timing, power, and routing information under specified libraries and constraints. Field-programmable gate array (FPGA) prototypes and fabricated silicon provide further observations, with their own measurement conditions and limits.

For a candidate schedule, the compiler's intermediate representation may expose tile dimensions and data reuse, while a simulator reports execution cycles, transfers, and stalls. The latency is a possible prediction target; transfers and stalls help explain it. An input-output comparison checks whether the schedule still computes the required result. Joining these sources by candidate and workload identity creates a more useful sample than storing an isolated timing number. It also identifies what is missing: a kernel simulation alone cannot establish whether the complete extended-reality (XR) frame meets its deadline.

Expert judgment supplies information that measurements alone may not explain. A review can identify an integration constraint, a schedule compromise, or a reason to reject an otherwise promising alternative. To reuse that judgment, a later reader needs the evidence considered, the criteria applied, and the limits of the conclusion. A provisional approximation should remain distinguishable from a checked result (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).

Together, these sources describe what a useful collection could contain. The next question is how much of it already exists in accessible datasets, and how much must be acquired for the intended study.

## Public Datasets and Their Limits {#sec-public-architecture-datasets}

Before collecting new data, we should examine what existing datasets can contribute. A useful collection need not contain everything a study requires, but its observations must match the part of the task we intend to use it for. The main questions are what each sample represents, which properties were evaluated, and what additional information would be needed for our study. The collections in @tbl-public-architecture-data illustrate these differences.

| **Collection and observation unit** | **Supported task** | **Key missing context** | **Failed or rejected data status** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenRTLSet observes one extracted Verilog module from public Verilog, VHDL, or high-level synthesis (HLS) C/C++ [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. | Fine-tuning and evaluating module-level Verilog generation. | Full project state, workload and software conditions, physical measurements, per-module functional checks, and repository-disjoint splits. | Failed VHDL and Vitis HLS conversions are excluded. No corpus of failed artifacts and rejection reasons is released. |
| RTL-Repo observes one target-line completion with surrounding Verilog repository context [@AllamShalan2024RTLRepo]. | Long-context, multi-file Verilog autocompletion evaluated with exact match and edit similarity. | Functional, synthesis, simulation, workload, power, performance, area, and physical-design evidence. Train and test counts do not establish a repository-disjoint split. | No design tool is executed for the observation. Repositories rejected by collection filters are not retained. |
| CircuitNet observes one back-end design run and retained layout under declared synthesis and physical-design settings [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet]. | Cross-stage congestion, design rule check violation, and IR-drop prediction from graph and image-like features. | Front-end software and workload behavior, live project history, and canonical grouping rules. | 12,960 runs attempted; 10,242 layouts retained after excluding failures. Failure causes are not retained. |
| QuArch v0.1 observes one expert-validated multiple-choice question-answer pair about computer architecture [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch]. | Evaluating architecture knowledge retrieval and fine-tuning language models for retrieval. | Executable design state, workload and software identity, tool returns, physical measurements, and signoff evidence. | Questions without definitive answers or with narrow scope are removed and not retained. |
: **A dataset supports only the task and context carried by its observations.** Module code, repository context, executed layouts, and architecture questions serve distinct purposes and leave different parts of design decisions unobserved. {#tbl-public-architecture-data tbl-colwidths="[28,20,26,26]"}

Each collection supports a different use because it observes a different part of design work. Module-generation datasets can help repair errors in generated Verilog [@LiuEtAl2024CraftRTL], but module text does not record the resulting implementation's congestion or supply-grid IR-drop.[^fn-ir-drop-c04] Layout datasets provide those physical observations without necessarily retaining the software behavior or algorithmic intent that produced the design. The table places each collection's capabilities beside its missing context and rejected-data policy so that sample count does not stand in for suitability.

Collection sizes also need to be read in their own units. Text corpora count tokens, while hardware datasets may count modules, layouts, or questions. OpenRTLSet contains roughly $1.3\times10^5$ Verilog modules [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet], CircuitNet reports on the order of $10^4$ retained layouts [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet], and QuArch contains question-answer pairs in the low thousands [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch]. These counts describe different kinds of examples. Their ratios do not measure how much useful information one collection supplies relative to another.

Missing context is not necessarily poor data quality. QuArch evaluates architecture knowledge without describing a live project, and CircuitNet provides physical-design observations without recording software behavior. The relevant test is whether the available information supports the intended use. A dataset can be useful for one component of a design workflow while leaving other observations to be collected separately.

Availability also reflects the work required to construct a collection. Public code may need several transformations before it yields even a synthesizable hardware artifact. The OpenRTLSet C/C++ collection path in @fig-public-code-to-rtl shows how an initially large pool narrows through screening and tool conversion.

```{python}
#| label: fig-public-code-to-rtl
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Building a Verilog corpus from public C/C++ code involves several filters.** The horizontal log-scale bar chart traces repository attrition in the OpenRTLSet C/C++ collection pipeline: approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories narrow to approximately 12,000 after synthesizability screening, and only approximately 1,000 successfully generate Verilog through Vitis HLS [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. The resulting 24,000 Verilog modules represent a distinct observation unit from the repositories shown. These counts reflect pipeline-specific tool filters rather than universal hardware synthesizability rates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale horizontal bar chart showing three stages from the OpenRTLSet C and C++ collection pipeline. Approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories enter the pipeline, 12,000 remain after the authors' synthesizability screen, and 1,000 successfully generate Verilog through Vitis HLS."

# Empirical repository counts extracted from OpenRTLSet dataset collection pipeline [WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

stages = [
    "Permissively licensed\nC/C++ repositories",
    "After authors'\nsynthesizability screen",
    "Successful Vitis HLS\nto Verilog",
]
counts = [103_000, 12_000, 1_000]
display_counts = ["≈103,000", "≈12,000", "≈1,000"]
y = [2, 1, 0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.7, 2.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.38, right=0.92, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(400, 300_000)

bars = ax.barh(
    y,
    counts,
    left=400,
    height=0.42,
    color=COLORS["workload"],
    edgecolor=COLORS["note_edge"],
    linewidth=0.8,
    zorder=2,
)

for x_value, y_value, label in zip(counts, y, display_counts):
    ax.text(
        (400 + x_value) * 1.15,
        y_value,
        label,
        ha="left",
        va="center",
        fontsize=6.4,
        fontweight="bold",
        color=COLORS["workload_ink"],
    )

ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(stages, fontsize=6.2)
ax.set_xlabel("approximate repositories remaining (log scale)", fontsize=6.2)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, pad=5)
ax.grid(axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=1)

for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
```

The collection starts from permissively licensed repositories, screens for synthesizability, and then attempts conversion with Vitis HLS [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. The surviving repositories provide generated Verilog modules, not a matching set of physical implementations and workload measurements. This is a concrete form of hardware-data scarcity: the code needed to begin a collection can be available while the observations needed for a particular engineering question still require substantial work. The reported attrition describes this collection procedure, rather than a universal rate at which public programs can become hardware.

A foundation model pretrained on open repositories can learn syntax, circuit idioms, and documented design rules.[^fn-foundation-model-c04] The scarcity of complete implementations limits what that training alone establishes about applying those rules under project conditions. Assessing clock-domain crossings for metastability risk,[^fn-metastability-c04] managing power-grid voltage drops, and preventing combinational loops still require checks on the proposed design. This distinction connects corpus quality to the evaluation bottleneck in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales: generating a plausible artifact and qualifying it consume different resources.

[^fn-metastability-c04]: **Metastability**: A transient state in which a storage element has not resolved to a valid logic level within the expected time. A setup or hold violation, including one caused by an asynchronous input, can produce it. Synchronizers reduce the probability that unresolved behavior reaches downstream logic; they do not eliminate the possibility of metastability.

[^fn-foundation-model-c04]: **Foundation model**: A model pretrained on broad data at scale and then adapted to many downstream tasks rather than trained for a single one [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels]. The term comes from machine learning, and this chapter treats such a model as one optional component inside a design system rather than as the design system itself.

Internal project data can fill some gaps, subject to the access restrictions discussed in @sec-architecture-data-access. ChipNeMo illustrates task-specific domain adaptation using proprietary chip-design material for engineering assistance, EDA script generation, and bug summarization [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. Its use of internal material does not make that material publicly reproducible; an evaluation must state which evidence an independent reviewer can inspect.

For the Lighthouse mapping study, the remaining gap is specific. Neither architecture question-answer pairs nor physical-layout observations supply the schedule-latency pairs needed to compare software on the candidate NPU. Those observations would have to be acquired or adapted from a compatible source. The source kernels, candidate schedules, hardware target, correctness checks, and execution results must be connected before the collection can support that comparison.

Public availability therefore answers only part of the data question. Once we know what existing sources contribute, we can identify the missing observations and choose how to obtain them at a cost and coverage appropriate to the study.

## Collecting Architectural Data

When existing datasets do not contain the observations a study needs, those observations must be collected. The collection plan has three connected choices: the path used to evaluate a candidate, the resources required to obtain a result, and the workloads or operating conditions covered. In the Lighthouse mapping study, even a software-only schedule change may require new compilation and execution. More detailed evaluation can answer more demanding questions, but its cost limits how broadly it can be used.

### Choosing an Observation Path

The required observation determines the evaluation path. For the Lighthouse mapping study, comparing schedules requires execution results from a model or implementation that represents the relevant computation and data movement. Estimating the physical cost of the accelerator requires additional implementation information. A tool may answer one question well while leaving another unresolved. The alternatives in @tbl-observation-source-limits therefore differ in what they observe, which assumptions they make, and what obtaining a result costs.

| **Source** | **Useful for** | **Important limit to represent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical model | Fast sensitivity studies and early bounds. | Simplifying equations, calibration range, and omitted interactions. |
| SystemC / transaction-level modeling (TLM) 2.0 virtual platform | Rapid transaction-level memory and interconnect throughput exploration and early software bring-up. | Pin-level clock timing, detailed gate delays, layout parasitics, and unmodeled contention. |
| Trace-driven simulator (ChampSim, Ramulator 2) | Repeatable study of memory access streams, cache hierarchies, and DRAM bus scheduling under captured workloads. | No timing feedback absent from the trace, and no unmodeled bus states. |
| Cycle-level simulator (gem5, SCALE-Sim) | Detailed modeled microarchitectural behavior across CPU cores, NPU accelerators, and interconnects. | Simulator abstractions, unsupported states, calibration, and execution cost. |
| Gate-level netlist simulation | Pin-level logic verification, cell delay evaluation, and X-propagation (the rippling of unknown or uninitialized states through logic gates) under synthesized netlists. | Testbench coverage, runtime overhead, timing abstractions, and unmodeled layout parasitics. |
| RTL simulation (Verilator, VCS) | Logic, interface, and microarchitectural behavior over the exercised testbench. | Stimulus identity, functional coverage, simulator version, and unmodeled physical delays. |
| Formal analysis (SystemVerilog Assertions / bounded model checking) | Proof, counterexample, bounded-only, or inconclusive status for a stated property and assumptions. | Stated property, assumptions, abstraction, proof method, bound, vacuity checks, and status. |
| Synthesis and STA / power analysis (Yosys, Design Compiler, OpenSTA) | Logic transformation, technology mapping, and static timing analysis (STA), area, or power estimates within the flow. | Libraries, modes, corners, constraints, tool versions, and physical approximations. |
| Place-and-route and physical verification (OpenROAD, Innovus) | Placement, routing, extraction, timing, power integrity, and design rule checking (DRC) results for the implemented database. | Floorplan state, signoff models, modes, corners, waivers, tool versions, and manufacturing models. |
| FPGA or emulation platform | High-throughput functional or timing-model execution after mapping. | Mapping differences, compile cost, debug visibility, and non-transferable application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) power or timing. |
| Fabricated silicon | Behavior of a physical implementation under measured conditions. | Limited design variants, observability, stepping, test conditions, and inability to answer counterfactual questions. |
: **Every observation source has a useful scope and a blind spot.** Recording both ensures appropriate tool selection and qualification in downstream chapters. {#tbl-observation-source-limits tbl-colwidths="[22,36,42]"}

A timing closure report from a gate-level netlist cannot substitute for a power integrity analysis of the routed layout. Similarly, a transaction-level model that omits arbitration or flit serialization cannot supply cycle-exact packet latency under contention. A method needs these limits attached to each observation so it can distinguish a useful proxy from a result about the target property.

Hardware measurements depend on the conditions under which they were obtained. In an illustrative multiplier example, suppose a timing analysis reports a 1.1\ ns cycle time at an assumed typical corner (0.85\ V, $25^\circ\text{C}$). A second assumed corner (0.72\ V, $125^\circ\text{C}$) or different clock-tree skew may change whether that implementation closes timing.[^fn-timing-closure-c04] These values illustrate the context a record must retain; they are not measurements of a particular multiplier or foundry process, and they do not determine the size of a timing violation. A timing label is therefore incomplete without the implementation and analysis conditions that produced it.

An evaluated candidate can be described by the context-bound tuple $\mathcal{O} = \langle s_{\text{design}}, w_{\text{workload}}, \tau_{\text{tool}}, \kappa_{\text{corner}}, y_{\text{metrics}} \rangle$. Here $s_{\text{design}}$ denotes the microarchitectural and RTL configuration together with the candidate's software choices; $w_{\text{workload}}$ identifies the application inputs, execution phase, and matching binary; $\tau_{\text{tool}}$ identifies the compiler and evaluation toolchain; $\kappa_{\text{corner}}$ specifies the process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions where applicable; and $y_{\text{metrics}}$ contains the returned measurements. In the mapping study, a latency without its schedule and hardware target is incomplete. A power estimate additionally needs the implementation and activity assumptions that produced it. The tuple describes these dependencies without implying that every source already supplies every field.

### The Cost of a Useful Sample

For the mapping study, acquisition begins before the timed execution. A candidate schedule must compile for the target, pass the required output checks, and be loaded into the evaluation environment. A simulator or hardware run then supplies latency and any diagnostic counters. Preparing the compiler backend or calibrating the accelerator model is a shared setup cost; compilation, testing, execution, and diagnosis contribute costs per candidate. Repeated runs and additional workload shapes expand that cost. A dataset budget that counts only the final timing call misses much of the work needed to produce a usable label.

The effect of execution coverage can be quantified independently of a particular Lighthouse candidate. Consider an illustrative 1\ GHz target, a 1\ s measured interval, 0.2\ s of warmup, a simulator rate of 100,000 target cycles per wall-clock second, three repetitions, and four workloads.

```{python}
#| echo: false

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter4-simulation-time-explosion.csv

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(
    _root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter4-simulation-time-explosion.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",
) as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    _simulation_cost_rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))

_one_second_row = next(
    row
    for row in _simulation_cost_rows
    if row["target_workload_duration"] == "1 s"
)
measurement_cycles = int(_one_second_row["target_cycles_at_1ghz"])
warmup_cycles = measurement_cycles // 5
simulator_rate = 100_000
repetitions = 3
workloads = 4
single_measurement_hours = measurement_cycles / simulator_rate / 3_600
total_target_cycles = (
    (warmup_cycles + measurement_cycles) * repetitions * workloads
)
total_serial_hours = total_target_cycles / simulator_rate / 3_600
assert _one_second_row["wall_time_at_100kcycle_s"] == "2.8 h"
assert round(total_target_cycles / 1e9, 1) == 14.4
assert round(total_serial_hours) == 40
```

During a single measured interval of 1\ s, a 1\ GHz target executes one billion cycles ($10^9$). At an assumed simulator rate of 100,000 target cycles per wall-clock second, simulating that single second demands roughly 2.8\ hours. Serial execution cost $T_{\text{serial}}$ combines target warmup cycles $C_{\text{warmup}}$, target measurement cycles $C_{\text{measure}}$, repetition count $R$, workload count $W$, and simulator throughput $v_{\text{sim}}$:

$$
T_{\text{serial}} =
\frac{(C_{\text{warmup}} + C_{\text{measure}}) \times R \times W}
{v_{\text{sim}}}.
$${#eq-serial-execution-cost}

Under the assumptions in @eq-serial-execution-cost, evaluating four workloads across three repetitions executes 14.4 billion target cycles and consumes forty serial simulator hours.

These forty hours describe accumulated simulator runtime. Parallel execution can shorten the elapsed collection time when resources permit, but it does not remove the required evaluations. Shared setup, compilation, correctness checks, queueing, and diagnosis add costs beyond this execution estimate.

Even if a surrogate evaluated a candidate in an illustrative two milliseconds, it would still need reference observations for training or calibration, whose acquisition can consume days of cluster compute. In BOOM-Explorer, for example, high-fidelity VLSI flow evaluations across 994 microarchitectural configurations required between six and fourteen hours per candidate [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. At those costs, a sweep across millions of variations would require a different acquisition strategy or budget.

Recording resource use alongside the results helps the team budget further collection. Execution time, memory requirements, license demand, and human effort can make different evaluation paths practical at different scales. The result's conditions and check status explain what that expenditure established. Together, these details let a later user judge both whether an observation is useful and what obtaining comparable observations would cost (@tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels).

| **Dataset simplification** | **Architecture sample** | **Consequence for later use** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cheap acquisition** | Results require scarce licenses, long tool runs, fabrication, setup, diagnosis, and expert review. | Records must capture resources and human work required to obtain the result. |
| **Fixed ground-truth label** | Tools return results for named properties at stated fidelities under recorded conditions. | Properties, checks, fidelities, and conditions must be preserved for interpretation. |
| **Independent, interchangeable rows** | Results frequently share ancestors, generated artifacts, traces, images, seeds, or earlier decisions. | Lineage must be preserved to avoid counting dependent results as independent support. |
| **Missing data without structure** | Failed, timed-out, and rejected runs are selectively lost; some violations reveal only threshold crossings. | Run status, failure reasons, and censored bounds must be retained rather than learning only from survivors. |
| **Matching attributes imply comparability** | Two rows support comparison only when candidate identities, permitted differences, workloads, and tool paths match. | Results with uncontrolled differences must be treated as advisory context rather than matched comparisons. |
: **Architecture samples are costly, conditioned results.** Their meaning and comparability depend on lineage, property checks, acquisition status, and matched study conditions. {#tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

### Choosing Workload Coverage

Once the cost of an evaluation is visible, the next question is which executions deserve that budget. Static descriptions identify what a system can execute; workloads determine which paths become active, which queues saturate, and which memory banks stall. A short trace is useful only if it captures behavior relevant to the target question.

For Lighthouse's XR workload, a kernel measurement needs its input shape, data type, and schedule, while a frame measurement also needs the surrounding stages and their overlap. The subsystem's 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope applies to the work within that system boundary. A fast isolated kernel may still wait for inputs or contend with rendering when integrated. The dataset should distinguish isolated-kernel observations from frame-level observations instead of treating both as labels for the same target.

Coverage must also match the outcome being evaluated. A collection designed to estimate average throughput may miss brief stalls that determine whether a frame meets its deadline. Before selecting representative intervals, we need to identify which workload behaviors could change the architectural conclusion.

System performance, power dissipation, and thermal behavior are joint outcomes $y = f(x, w)$ of the hardware configuration $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and the dynamic workload feature vector $w \in \mathcal{W}$. Altering the application software or workload phase can shift a hardware candidate from compute-bound to memory-bound. To expose workload behavior without full-trace simulation overhead, execution traces are transformed into compact feature representations.

SimPoint constructs basic block vectors ($w_{\text{BBV}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$) by recording the dynamic execution frequency of each static basic block during fixed execution intervals (e.g., $10^7$ or $10^8$ instructions), weighted by static instruction count and normalized across the interval [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint]. Applying dimensionality reduction (such as random projection) and $k$-means clustering across interval vectors identifies recurring execution phases, allowing a small set of weighted simulation intervals (SimPoints) to estimate full-trace behavior.

The selected intervals' accuracy must be assessed for the target metrics; clustering alone does not supply a general error bound. SMARTS computes statistical confidence bounds over sampled execution slices under its sampling assumptions [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS].

In emerging workloads, dynamic phase features extend to transformer key-value (KV) cache footprints and decoding burst lengths. These workload features serve as dynamic environmental representations ($s_{\text{env}}$) conditioning microarchitectural evaluation.

Basic block vectors, memory stride histograms, and phase embeddings serve two primary representation roles in automated evaluation pipelines:

1. **Surrogate model conditioning vectors:** Supplying dynamic workload context $w$ to learned performance predictors across diverse software applications.
2. **Dynamic environment state encodings:** Supplying environment state $s_{\text{env}}$ in closed design loops (@sec-hardware-representation-formats) to reason about phase-dependent bottlenecks.

Compiler changes also affect what can be reused. A new tiling or scheduling choice may change the memory-access stream, so replaying the old schedule's trace would not evaluate the new one. The workload inputs and comparison interval can remain matched while each candidate produces its own trace. Basic block vectors likewise retain their association with the compiled image, collection policy, frame identifiers, and execution parameters. This distinction becomes especially useful when comparing a software-changing study with a cache study that holds the software image fixed.

### Connecting Results to Their Context

The observation path, acquisition cost, and workload coverage must remain connected in each sample. The separate Lighthouse cache comparison introduced in @sec-architecture-20-ontology provides a compact example of recording that context. Its software is fixed while capacity changes. The fragment in @lst-ch04-state-tuple shows design state $s_{\text{design}}$ and environmental state $s_{\text{env}}$ (encoding the workload context). Its identifiers and feature values are placeholders, including the static random-access memory (SRAM) name; they identify neither a retained execution nor a verified foundry macro. An actual observation would replace them with resolved artifact identities and captured workload features.

```{.json #lst-ch04-state-tuple lst-cap="Illustrative serialized state fragment with placeholder identities and values; no Lighthouse execution is represented."}
{
  "s_design": {
    "commit_hash": "a1b2c3d4",
    "module": "l2_cache_subsystem",
    "parameters": {
      "l2.capacity": "3MiB",
      "sram_macro": "TSMC_N3E_HD_1R1W_3MB"
    }
  },
  "s_env": {
    "workload": "xr_slam_tracking",
    "software_image": "lighthouse_os_v1.4",
    "frame_bounds": [840, 860],
    "w_bbv": [0.12, 0.05, 0.88, 0.0]
  }
}
```

The remaining fields specify what an execution would have to return. The tool state $\tau_{\text{tool}}$ would pin the simulator and implementation toolchain; $\kappa_{\text{corner}}$ would name the TSMC N3E conditions used for an SRAM evaluation. The requested vector $y_{\text{metrics}}$ includes 99th-percentile frame time in milliseconds, subsystem power in watts against the 3\ W ceiling, macro area in square millimeters against the $1.5\text{ mm}^2$ limit, and access time in nanoseconds against the 2.5\ ns limit. Each returned value would retain its acquisition source, check status, and wall-clock and license cost. No such measurements have been collected for this study.

The comparison keys would link study revision, design revision, candidate configuration, workload snapshot, software image, toolchain manifest, and physical conditions. Matched rows must agree on the fixed conditions while tracing any design differences to the permitted capacity change. If a run times out or fails to route, the record retains these identities and any qualified partial results, marks missing metrics as unavailable, and records the failure class. Missing values must not become artificial low scores.

## Constructing Architecture Datasets

A collection procedure explains how to obtain one observation. Constructing a dataset requires deciding which observations belong together, which parts of the design space they should cover, and how to keep their meaning intact. The acquisition costs just derived limit that coverage. Accumulating convenient simulation logs and Verilog files may leave the cases that distinguish competing designs unobserved.

For the Lighthouse mapping study, the collection plan should cover the operator shapes and schedules that could change the conclusion. Evaluating many tile sizes on one convenient matrix shape may leave the rest of the perception workload poorly represented. A useful initial collection would include different reuse patterns and working-set sizes, including cases near the target's memory limits. The plan should also reserve evaluations for checking whether an apparent kernel improvement survives integration into the frame workload.

Dataset adequacy depends on whether the observations resolve the intended comparison. More repetitions help characterize run-to-run variation; new input shapes address a coverage gap; another hardware target tests a different kind of transfer. These uses compete for the same acquisition budget and cannot substitute for one another. In the smaller cache study, the corresponding question is whether matched runs distinguish the 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB candidates from the 2\ MiB baseline, with each candidate also checked against the SRAM constraints. If the available observations cannot resolve a comparison, the next sample should address the uncertainty that prevents a decision.

### Multi-Fidelity Sampling

*Multi-fidelity sampling* combines inexpensive estimates with more costly evaluations, such as analytical bounds with cycle-level simulation or implementation results. The sources must estimate the same output or have an explicit relationship between their outputs [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. Sharing a candidate identity does not make their results interchangeable. Active learning can help allocate further observations, selecting examples expected to improve a model or resolve uncertainty within the available budget [@Settles2009ActiveLearning]. Its usefulness depends on whether those selections repay their acquisition cost.

For the mapping study, inexpensive estimates could screen many schedules, while more costly evaluations examine selected candidates near constraint boundaries or decision crossovers. The dataset must retain which source produced each result so that an analytical estimate does not become indistinguishable from an execution measurement. Unobserved regions remain unsupported. Selection policies must record rules, candidate pools, and available observations to preserve evaluation boundaries [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout].

### Dataset Integrity and Construction Pipelines

Collection produces artifacts and tool returns; curation makes their relationships usable. In the mapping dataset, a row can identify one kernel, input shape, schedule, and target, then link to its compiled artifact, correctness result, repeated timings, and diagnostic counters. Units must be consistent, repetitions must remain grouped, and missing results must remain distinguishable from measured zeros. The source kernel and transformation history also provide grouping keys for evaluation splits. Holding out new schedules for a familiar kernel tests a different capability from holding out an operator family that never appeared in training.

Treating training examples as independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) is a modeling assumption, not a property guaranteed by storing them in a table. Multiple results may share a design ancestor, generated artifact, workload trace, or software image. Repeated evaluations of one schedule can estimate variation without supplying independent programs. Grouping these relationships explicitly makes it possible to test the intended kind of transfer and prevents a large row count from disguising a narrow set of designs.

Protected evaluation splits must follow the transfer claim (family, workload, software revision, or time period) rather than random row partitioning [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage]. Parameterized hardware description language (HDL) generators make this distinction especially important. Different configurations can reuse the same subgraphs, so a split that separates rows but shares their generating templates may test recognition of those templates rather than generalization to another design family.

Pipeline construction must also address *data contamination*. Exposure to public hardware benchmarks during training can inflate evaluation scores through memorization rather than demonstrate the intended generation capability [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated; @Balloccu2024Leakage]. Private testbenches, repository-disjoint splits, and behavior-preserving transformations of test artifacts address different exposure risks. No one measure is mandatory or sufficient for every study. The dataset should state which exposure paths were examined, what each measure protects, and whether the transformed tasks still test the claimed capability.

Synthetic training examples need checks matched to their intended use. Treating unverified generator outputs as measured or verified observations can mislead downstream learning [@VanBreugelEtAl2023SyntheticData]. Methods like CraftRTL use synthetic Verilog examples to repair model errors [@LiuEtAl2024CraftRTL], but passing syntax checks does not establish functional behavior, and passing functional tests does not establish timing or power. A dataset can retain examples at each status, provided it records the generator identity, intended task, and checks performed. Physical evaluation is needed when the label makes a physical claim.

Even when examples are selected and checked carefully, the construction pipeline can introduce errors while extracting or combining results. The term *data cascades* describes how upstream data problems can produce delayed consequences in downstream work [@SambasivanEtAl2021DataCascades; @NorthcuttJiangChuang2021ConfidentLearning]. In architecture, a parser that reads negative timing slack as zero or classifies license exhaustion as design failure can turn tool returns into misleading training signals. An unrecorded compiler flag or transformation may also change the comparison's meaning without appearing in the dataset. Linking computed attributes to raw returns and recorded derivations lets a reviewer detect such errors and determine which conclusions they affect.

### Failed and Censored Runs

Dataset construction must preserve what an evaluation attempt established. A single pass/fail label cannot distinguish results with different implications for learning and reuse:

- *Infrastructure faults* (such as floating-license exhaustion or network interruption) identify problems with the execution environment. Repair and retry policy depends on the cause; these faults do not establish candidate infeasibility. A simulator crash needs diagnosis before it belongs in this category.
- *Syntax and typing defects* (such as undeclared wires or bitwidth mismatches) identify errors in a proposed artifact. A repair may require changing the artifact, its generator, or the transformation that produced it.
- *Constraint violations* (such as negative setup slack, unroutability, or exceeded power delivery network (PDN) IR-drop limits) identify a failed requirement under the recorded implementation and tool conditions. They constrain reuse under those conditions without proving that every implementation of the architecture must fail.
- *Formal verification results* distinguish proofs, counterexamples, bounded results, and inconclusive returns. Each retains its property, assumptions, and proof scope; a bounded check does not establish behavior beyond its horizon.
- *Resource-limit stops* retain the elapsed budget, partial results, and unresolved property. A timeout may reflect candidate complexity, tool behavior, or infrastructure; the status alone does not identify which.

For a compiler-generated schedule, producing the wrong output is different from failing to obtain a compiler license or exhausting an execution budget. A fast but incorrect schedule cannot be labeled a successful performance improvement. An unexplained compiler crash does not establish that the schedule is impossible on the hardware. Retaining the inputs, raw returns, and classification keeps these distinctions available for diagnosis and later training.

In physical design, a measured timing or routing violation provides information near a feasibility boundary under the tested conditions. Training a surrogate exclusively on successful signoff runs introduces survivorship bias [@Rubin1976InferenceMissingData], because the optimizer never sees where those attempts failed. Retaining unsuccessful attempts repairs that omission only if their status remains distinguishable.

A censored observation establishes a bound on a named quantity rather than its exact value.[^fn-censored-c04] It might establish $y \ge y_{\text{limit}}$ for latency, for example, but a tool timeout alone supplies no such bound on circuit latency. How a method uses qualified labels and bounds belongs to method selection (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

[^fn-censored-c04]: **Censored observation**: The result establishes only that a value lies above or below a threshold rather than reporting the value itself [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival]. A failed target-frequency test is left-censored because it establishes that maximum sustainable frequency lies below the target.

A versioned execution history separates attempt status, candidate outcome, and project updates to prevent cleaning routines from conflating tool failures with design evidence (@fig-execution-history). Preserving all three allows a later reader to distinguish a completed check that rejected a candidate from an aborted attempt that left it unresolved.

![**Execution history tracking preserves status, outcome, and cost attributes.** The execution record tracks three independent dimensions across every evaluation attempt: attempt status (tool execution completion vs. failure), candidate outcome (qualification, rejection, or unresolved evidence for the active comparison), and project update (whether authoritative repository state changed). In the illustrated trace, Attempt 1 succeeds and commits an updated project revision; Attempt 2 completes but rejects the candidate, leaving baseline state intact; and Attempt 3 runs on stale inputs, producing no usable comparison outcome. Conceptual schema for execution provenance.](images/fig-execution-history){#fig-execution-history width="100%"
fig-alt="Versioned execution history with separate attempt status, candidate outcome, and project update attributes. One completed attempt advances a candidate and creates a new project version. A second completed attempt leaves the candidate rejected or unresolved and makes no project update. A third attempt completes on stale inputs, which yields no usable candidate outcome for the current comparison and leaves project state unchanged."}

In the mapping study, an old schedule's result can remain useful training material while no longer supplying a matched comparison for a new compiler release. Its value depends on the intended reuse and the conditions that changed. Keeping the execution history preserves that choice without presenting an old result as a current measurement.

The information extracted from a failed evaluation depends directly on its underlying failure mechanism (@tbl-negative-traces). Preserving root-cause diagnostics helps search algorithms distinguish setup issues from design violations under the tested conditions. Neither the failure label nor the diagnosis makes that boundary permanent when the design or conditions change.

| **Failed run or rejected alternative** | **Preserved information** | **How later work should use it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synthesis or timing violation** | Candidate, constraints, process assumptions, and failing paths. | Reconsider the candidate only after checking whether relevant conditions still apply. |
| **Unroutable or power failure** | Netlist, placement conditions, density, congestion, or IR-drop result. | Identify the affected region without treating the failure as characteristic of all similar designs. |
| **Proxy improvement overturned** | Cheap estimate, later observation, and precise divergence conditions. | Reassess the proxy's useful scope before attempting reuse. |
| **Tool failure or crash** | Command, inputs, environment identity, logs, and failure classification. | Diagnose the cause; repair infrastructure when established as the cause. Otherwise retain unresolved status until evidence supports classification. |
| **Coverage gap** | Missing workload, input, scenario, or architecture class. | Mark the strict boundary of the result rather than filling it with assumptions. |
| **Reviewer rejection** | Candidate, stated reason, risk, schedule, integration concern, and owner. | Preserve rationale and revisit only when relevant conditions fundamentally change. |
| **Waiver or exception** | Violated rule, justification, scope, owner, and expiration condition. | Prevent repeated work while keeping the granted exception visible. |
: **Rejected work remains useful when conditions are systematically recorded.** Explicit failure conditions allow subsequent architects to determine whether historical boundaries still apply. {#tbl-negative-traces tbl-colwidths="[26,34,40]"}

These outcomes can also suggest what to investigate next. In the mapping study, a schedule whose buffers exceed local-memory capacity could motivate a smaller tile or a different staging pattern. The diagnosed limitation gives the next experiment a purpose, while leaving open which revision will work.

## Extracting Architectural Knowledge from Raw Data

Curated observations establish what happened under particular conditions. Turning them into architectural knowledge requires explaining the result well enough to guide another decision. Suppose evaluations in the Lighthouse mapping study found that one schedule reduced both off-chip transfers and execution time on matched inputs. A plausible explanation is that its tiling kept intermediate data in local memory for reuse. The timing result alone would not establish that mechanism. Transfer counts, stall behavior, and the generated schedule would help test it against alternatives, such as a change in parallelism or instruction overhead. This is an illustrative interpretation, not a reported Lighthouse result.

The reusable lesson would describe when that schedule helps. It might apply to shapes whose working sets fit in the available local memory, while larger shapes require additional transfers and lose the benefit. Comparing those cases turns an isolated ranking into a conditional explanation. The supporting runs, counterexamples, and remaining uncertainty should stay linked to it. Otherwise, a later method may reuse the winning tile size after the workload or memory organization has changed, even though the reason it worked no longer applies.

*Raw data* records source observations, *durable knowledge* includes reusable design principles, checked specifications, and architectural explanations, and *live project state* identifies the hardware, software, workload, and constraints governing current work. These serve different purposes. A model may encode a useful scheduling pattern, but the active compiler configuration determines whether the current candidate actually uses it. The objects in @tbl-knowledge-objects therefore need source and freshness rules suited to their roles. Foundation-model weights can supply prior knowledge; they cannot identify current project state without access to its sources.

| **Object** | **Preserved state** | **Responsible source and freshness rule** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Trained-model weights** | Learned statistical regularities and general concepts. | Useful as prior knowledge, but never the source of record for active project state. |
| **Retrieval index / material** | Source-linked manuals, papers, examples, and project documents. | Underlying source remains responsible; version and date must match intended use. |
| **In-context working set** | Instructions, selected sources, current state, and operational examples. | Transient assembly; does not become project state until an update changes the responsible source. |
| **Defined comparison** | Question, comparator, scope, permitted changes, constraints, budget, and stop rules. | Authoritative comparison definition until the owner records a revision. |
| **Design / software artifacts** | Configuration, generated hardware, software images, manifests, and constraints. | Current only when authoritative sources agree and consistency checks pass. |
| **Workload state** | Trace, profile, population, phase definitions, sampling policy, and version. | Controls workload conditions only within recorded coverage. |
| **Project history** | Prior candidates, tool runs, failures, decisions, and rationale linked to conditions. | Records historical execution without making results applicable to current versions. |
: **Knowledge objects preserve distinct facts under explicit freshness rules.** Values derive from authoritative sources for each subsystem rather than from whichever context was supplied most recently. {#tbl-knowledge-objects tbl-colwidths="[20,34,46]"}

The freshness rule has to be enforced per object, because the objects age at different rates. If an obsolete constraint enters an active evaluation loop, the proposal and its checks can refer to different project revisions.[^fn-split-brain-c04] A generator pulls a bus width or clock frequency from outdated documentation while its proposal is meant to interface with the current implementation. The proposal can then be syntactically clean and internally consistent while violating the parameters governing the rest of the system (@fig-split-brain-causality).

![**Stale reference sources create phantom internal consistency in active design states.** When automated generators or retrieval systems query outdated specifications or unlinked historical logs, they generate candidate proposals that appear internally consistent while violating active project constraints (such as updated clock frequencies or revised bus widths). Cryptographic hash validation and version-freshness checks expose the mismatch before ungrounded proposals dispatch to costly downstream toolflows. Conceptual failure mechanism.](images/fig-split-brain-causality){#fig-split-brain-causality width="100%" fig-alt="A stale reference state and a current project state lead to an incompatible proposal. Version and freshness checks expose the mismatch before the proposal reaches a costly tool flow."}

In hardware, a stale interface assumption may survive syntax checks and logic synthesis if neither checks it against the current system. Discovering the mismatch after fabrication makes correction particularly costly. Regeneration from the responsible source and input-identity checks can expose the version mismatch before a proposal reaches an expensive toolchain. They do not establish interface compatibility by themselves; that still requires checks against the current design.

Maintaining current state incurs compute, storage, license, and review costs. A compiler release, new workload capture, or revised interface can make part of the available knowledge inapplicable. The team needs a way to detect these changes and decide which information to refresh. Keeping a smaller set of relevant sources current can be more useful than retaining a broad collection whose applicability is unclear.

With observations organized and their explanations qualified, the next decision is what a computational method should see. A useful explanation for an architect does not automatically supply the features a predictor needs or the operations a generator can change.

## Machine-Usable Hardware Representations {#sec-hardware-representation-formats}

The mapping dataset contains more information than every method will consume. A latency predictor might receive the operator shape, data type, loop organization, tile sizes, and target-memory features. The measured latency supplies its training target. Transfer counts and stalls can help explain the result, but measured counters are unsuitable inputs for a predictor intended to rank that candidate before execution unless a separate, available source supplies them. A feature representation must fit the point in the workflow where it will be used.

A generator needs a view it can change. A vector of tile sizes describes alternatives within a schedule template, but generating a different ordering or fusion of operations requires access to dependencies and supported transformations. The resulting proposal must map to compiler inputs and preserve the required numerical behavior. AutoTVM provides an established example of using program structure for prediction: its cost models use features extracted from low-level programs or learned representations of their syntax trees [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. The Lighthouse example applies the same data-design question to a prospective accelerator target; it does not assume that a trained model or backend is already available.

Hardware description languages illustrate the consequences of this choice. They encode concurrent circuits in text, but token order does not directly expose circuit connectivity or timing relationships. Two signals may sit far apart in a file while sharing a critical path. A method consuming RTL as tokens must recover those relationships; a graph can expose connectivity directly, while linked libraries and constraints supply electrical context absent from the RTL. Neither form alone establishes capacitive fanout loading, clock-domain crossing (CDC) safety, or setup-hold[^fn-setup-hold-c04] timing across physical operating corners.

An interface example shows why syntax alone is insufficient. A model might generate a plausible token sequence that connects incorrect signals, violates an interconnect protocol, drops a reset condition, or references a stale module hierarchy. Suppose a generated Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) Stream bridge must throttle its upstream sender when its first-in, first-out (FIFO) buffer fills, but omits the `tready` backpressure path. A simulation without congestion may miss the defect; bursts that exceed the receiver's service and buffering capacity can expose data loss.[^fn-backpressure-c04] The defect depends on the interface requirements: a receiver that can always accept transfers need not provide that signal. More superficially similar text examples do not establish that a generated bridge satisfies its flow-control contract. Usable representations must preserve the structure and contextual conditions that allow tools or reviewers to catch such mistakes before silicon fabrication.

Representation choice and automation scope are separate decisions. The layers in @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration describe the scope of work and permitted interface changes, not a progression from text to graphs. Point assistance can consume a typed graph, and a system-scale workflow can include text-generating components. What matters here is whether each component's view exposes the relationships its task requires. Parameter schemas enumerate allowed configurations; abstract syntax trees (ASTs), control-data flow graphs (CDFGs), and multi-level intermediate representations such as Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) and MLIR expose control flow, tensor dependencies, and memory-hierarchy staging. Type checks can reject malformed transformations and incompatible operands early. Functional correctness and physical realization still require the checks those types do not express.

The relationships a method must recover become more demanding as designs grow beyond isolated benchmark modules. A parse of 1,513 SystemVerilog module declarations, drawn from six public repositories at pinned commits, compares those structural demands across benchmark and production-oriented RTL. The reference modules shipped with academic AI benchmarks (VerilogEval and RTLLM) carry a median of 168 concrete syntax nodes and 16 clean lines of code. Production-oriented open RTL (OpenTitan, CV32E40P, VeeR EL2, and BlackParrot) runs to a median of 1,125 nodes and 99 clean lines, a measured $6.7\times$ gap in source complexity (@fig-ch04-ast-complexity-cliff a) [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM]. Two sensitivity checks narrow that ratio without erasing it. Restricting the comparison to files the parser read without diagnostics yields $4.8\times$, and weighting each repository equally rather than each module yields $4.3\times$.

Structure separates the two populations more sharply than size does. No VerilogEval module instantiates another module in the corpus, so its hierarchy bottoms out at depth 1. RTLLM reaches a uniquely defined local child in 16% of its modules, to a maximum internal depth of 5. The production repositories reach one in 45% to 63% of their modules, to a maximum internal depth of 13 (@fig-ch04-ast-complexity-cliff b). Multiple clock-like event signals appear in 5.1% of production modules against 0.5% of benchmark modules, although that count indicates lexical clocking structure rather than a verified clock-domain crossing. A high score on flat leaf modules does not establish that a generator can preserve submodule interfaces across thirteen levels of instantiation. That capability needs a comparison that exercises the hierarchy.

![**Measured source complexity and internal hierarchy across 1,513 RTL modules.** (a) The cumulative distribution of concrete syntax nodes per module separates AI benchmark reference RTL (median 168 nodes, 217 modules) from production-oriented open RTL (median 1,125 nodes, 1,296 modules), a $6.7\times$ module-weighted median gap. (b) The share of modules reaching a uniquely defined local child rises from 0% in VerilogEval and 16% in RTLLM to between 45% and 63% across the production repositories, whose internal hierarchy reaches depth 13. Parsed with pyslang 11.0.0 from pinned commits [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM].](images/fig-ch04-ast-complexity-cliff){#fig-ch04-ast-complexity-cliff width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel figure comparing AI benchmark reference RTL with production-oriented open RTL. (a) Empirical cumulative distribution of concrete syntax nodes per module on a log scale, with the benchmark curve centered near 168 nodes and the production curve near 1,125 nodes, a 6.7 times median gap. (b) Horizontal bar chart of the share of modules that reach a uniquely defined local child, rising from 0 percent for VerilogEval and 16 percent for RTLLM to 45 to 63 percent for VeeR EL2, CV32E40P, BlackParrot, and OpenTitan."}

::: {.callout-law title="The Streetlight Effect in Hardware AI Benchmarks"}
**The Classical Principle:** Searching where measurement is convenient rather than where the truth or failure resides ($P(\text{search} \mid \text{easy}) \gg P(\text{search} \mid \text{true})$) [@Kaplan1964ConductOfInquiry].

**Evaluation Limitations:** The sampled benchmark modules are smaller and less hierarchical than the sampled production-oriented RTL. No VerilogEval module instantiates another module in the corpus, while 16% of RTLLM modules reach a uniquely defined local child. High success rates on these benchmarks alone do not establish capability in resolving structural interface bugs across deeper hierarchies.

**Evaluation Requirements:** Claims about generative tools for multi-clock system-on-chip (SoC) designs, hierarchical interconnects, or physical floorplans need evaluations that exercise those structures. An isolated-module benchmark remains useful for a task confined to that scope (@sec-law-streetlight-effect in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

Even within a leaf module, text order can conceal relationships a method needs. Software also has dependencies that cross statements and files; in hardware RTL, signals additionally connect concurrently active logic and state. Nearby declarations need not describe nearby circuit elements. When an automated method consumes hardware as a flat token sequence, it must recover connections whose endpoints may lie far apart in that sequence (@fig-ch04-spatial-semantic-dilation a).

This spatial-semantic dilation gap exposes a burden placed on sequence models, rather than establishing that they cannot handle larger blocks. A model must recover the connection between an AXI `tready` signal and its uses even when thousands of tokens separate them. Typed intermediate representations such as CIRCT MLIR can expose supported definition-use relationships directly through single static assignment (SSA) operand graphs. Whether that structure improves a particular model's reliability requires a controlled comparison. The measured Verilog side appears in @fig-ch04-spatial-semantic-dilation b, where semantic operators occupy $16\%$ to $27\%$ of tokens across six corpora. We have not measured token composition for a CIRCT corpus, so the typed-dialect side is a design intent rather than a result.

![**Spatial-semantic dilation across hardware representations.** (a) Definition-use distance across 344 open-source hardware modules (VerilogEval, RTLLM, BaseJump STL, and RISC-V cores). Topological AST distance holds at a median of one hop while linear token distance grows almost linearly in module scale ($\Delta_{\text{token}} \propto N^{0.99}$), opening a measured dilation gap up to $49{,}407\times$ [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM]. (b) Token allocation across the same six corpora, where syntactic boilerplate takes $49\%$ to $58\%$ of tokens and semantic operators take $16\%$ to $27\%$.](images/fig-hardware-representation-dilation){#fig-ch04-spatial-semantic-dilation width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel plot. (a) Log-log scatter of mean def-use distance against AST node count for 344 hardware modules, showing topological AST distance flat near one hop while linear token distance rises to thousands of tokens. (b) Horizontal stacked bar chart of token composition for VerilogEval, RTLLM, BaseJump STL, SERV, Ibex and PicoRV32, showing syntactic boilerplate between 49 and 58 percent of tokens."}

Representation structure can affect turnaround, but it does not determine compiler complexity by itself. Module boundaries and retained analyses may let a compiler avoid repeating work on unchanged parts of a design. Whether a pass can do so depends on its dependencies and invalidation rules, including relationships that cross module boundaries. A comparison of compilation or high-level synthesis (HLS) time therefore needs measurements on the chosen toolchain rather than a scaling guarantee inferred from the representation class.

CIRCT and MLIR provide domain-specific dialects for representing a computation at several abstraction levels [@CIRCT]. Tensor dialects such as `linalg` and `tosa` retain operations and shapes; `affine` represents structured loop bounds and access functions. The `scf` and `memref` dialects expose control flow and memory operations, while hardware dialects such as `hw`, `comb`, `seq`, `sv`, and `firrtl` express structural blocks, bitvector operations, state, and SystemVerilog constructs. These distinctions explain why the Lighthouse mapping study needs links between the computation, its software schedule, and the target hardware. A particular compiler chooses the transformations and backend needed to connect its supported levels; the availability of the dialects alone does not supply that implementation path. The independent fragments in @lst-mlir-circt-lowering illustrate what several levels can expose. Equality graphs, hypergraph netlists, and tokenized waveform streams are additional task-specific views; their use for rewriting, prediction, and estimation is developed with the methods in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization.

```{.mlir #lst-mlir-circt-lowering lst-cap="**Schematic representation fragments at three abstraction levels.** These nonexecuted excerpts show tensor operations, loop/memory accesses, and hardware primitives. Definitions and enclosing context are omitted. The floating-point tensor fragment and integer bitvector hardware fragment are not equivalent implementations or demonstrated stages of one lowering flow."}
// Tier 1: High-Level Tensor Dialect (linalg / tosa): Preserves loop bounds & shapes
%C = linalg.matmul ins(%A, %B : tensor<16x16xf16>, tensor<16x16xf16>)
                   outs(%C_init : tensor<16x16xf32>) -> tensor<16x16xf32>

// Tier 2: Bufferized Memory & Affine Dialect (memref / affine): Exposes SRAM allocations
affine.for %i = 0 to 16 {
  affine.for %j = 0 to 16 {
    %a_val = memref.load %sram_A[%i, %k] : memref<16x16xf16, 1>
    %b_val = memref.load %sram_B[%k, %j] : memref<16x16xf16, 1>
    // Explicit multiply-accumulate on local scratchpad memory buffers
  }
}

// Tier 3: Typed Hardware Dialect in CIRCT (hw / comb / seq): Bitvectors & clock domains
hw.module @npu_pe(in %clk : !seq.clock, in %rst : i1, in %a : i16, in %b : i16, out %acc : i32) {
  %a_ext = comb.concat %zero16, %a : i16, i16 -> i32
  %b_ext = comb.concat %zero16, %b : i16, i16 -> i32
  %prod  = comb.mul %a_ext, %b_ext : i32
  %sum   = comb.add %reg_out, %prod : i32
  %reg_out = seq.firreg %sum clock %clk sym @acc_reg : i32
  hw.output %reg_out : i32
}
```

The tensor fragment exposes dimensions and numerical types; the loop fragment exposes access indices and a memory space; the hardware fragment exposes arithmetic connected to state. They are independent excerpts. The integer hardware does not implement the floating-point tensor operation, and definitions such as `%k` and `%zero16` are omitted. A working lowering example would need complete definitions, compatible arithmetic and state semantics, and checks of the implemented transformation. For the Lighthouse mapping question, the useful distinction is what each view preserves. A method changing tiles needs dimensions and access relationships that may no longer be explicit in a lower-level artifact, so their connection to the source must remain recoverable.

SystemVerilog specifies logic, hierarchy, and verification constructs [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. Technology-mapped gate-level netlists identify library cells and pin-level connections; their timing analysis also needs cell models, constraints, and the relevant interconnect information. And-inverter graphs (AIGs) instead represent Boolean logic through AND nodes and complemented edges, without selecting a particular cell library. Microarchitectural traces (ChampSim, Ramulator 2) record memory events at the level exposed by their capture and simulation setup. Flexible Intermediate Representation for RTL (FIRRTL) and typed CIRCT dialects expose compiler operations and transformations [@CIRCT; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel]. Companion formats like Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) and Unified Power Format (UPF) carry timing and power intent [@SynopsysSDC; @IEEE2024UPF]. Each representation format makes specific properties explicit while leaving other constraints for downstream checks (@tbl-representation-formats).

| **Artifact or representation** | **What it makes explicit** | **What it hides, and the blind spot that follows** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paper, plot, manual, or specification | Concepts, requirements, interfaces, reported claims, and source-linked rationale. | The current project version, whether a local implementation satisfies the requirement, tool flags, failed candidates, and tuning history; the endpoint is visible but the path cannot be reconstructed. |
| Design note, review note, or Q&A | Judgment, calculations, rationale, risk, and the decision taken. | Executable state and the assumptions or alternatives never written down; later work remembers verdicts but not conditions. |
| Source AST (Clang) | Source-language declarations, expressions, types, and syntax structure. | Lowered scheduling, register allocation, and target execution behavior. |
| Software compiler IR (LLVM, Triton dialects) | Operations and control/data dependencies at the dialect's level; supported tensor and thread-layout choices. | Execution properties not modeled at that level, including physical timing and workload-dependent stalls. |
| Virtual instruction set (CUDA PTX) | Typed virtual instructions, registers, memory operations, and thread behavior. | Final target instruction selection, physical register allocation, and measured execution timing. |
| NPU CDFG or MLIR spatial dialect | Tensor dataflow dependencies, loop tilings, operator fusion, and scratchpad staging. | Host-to-NPU transfer latency, gate-level timing, thermal throttling, and power-grid drops; the schedule bottlenecks on system data delivery. |
| SystemVerilog / VHDL source | Logic, hierarchy, interfaces, declared types and widths, and parameter values, interpreted through language semantics and elaboration. | Behavior outside the tests performed, external requirements, and physical properties supplied by libraries, constraints, and implementation tools. |
| Typed hardware IR (FIRRTL, CIRCT) | Operations, types, connectivity, and supported transformations. | Which legal designs are expressible, semantic correctness, lowering, and physical realization. |
| SystemC / TLM 2.0 virtual platform | Transaction-level memory and interconnect behavior, sockets, and early software bring-up. | Pin-accurate timing, clock-cycle delays, and gate or layout parasitics. |
| Technology-mapped gate-level netlist | Selected library cells and pin-level connections. | Architectural intent, functional correctness, and physical context supplied separately by libraries, constraints, and parasitics. |
| And-inverter graph (AIG) | Boolean logic structure through AND nodes and complemented edges. | Cell-library mapping, electrical delay, and physical layout; Boolean structure alone does not establish timing. |
| Memory or microarchitectural trace (ChampSim, Ramulator) | Observed instruction execution, cache miss streams, and DRAM bank and rank commands. | Behavior outside the captured population, the sampling policy, OS page translation, and timing feedback; the hierarchy is tuned to a static trace. |
| Parameter schema / generator | Mutable parameters, legal values, and reproducible lowering paths. | Agreement between generator and checked-in artifacts, and the dependent collateral each change must update. |
| SDC, UPF, and constraints | Timing and power intent, domains, path references, and implementation assumptions. | Hierarchical-name coupling, stale paths, waived checks, and RTL consistency. |
| Simulator configuration or tool run and report | A result under a named design, tool, configuration, seed, model, and workload. | Defaults, unsupported states, calibration limits, process assumptions, and waived warnings; the number is trusted outside the tool's useful scope, and no general rule follows from it. |
| Graph, spatial, or cross-layer mapping | Connectivity, topology, adjacency, physical location, and links from architecture choices to lower objects. | Properties omitted from nodes and edges, write-back to tool inputs, and intermediate transformations nobody recorded; a physical failure cannot be traced to the choice that caused it. |
| Learned embedding vector | Task-dependent learned features and similarity relationships. | Exact structure, identity, units, legality, and check status unless supplied separately; encoded correlations do not certify these properties. |
| Rejected candidate or review decision | A boundary that mattered, the conditions that exposed it, and why work stopped. | Whether the rejection still applies after the design or conditions change, and the failure reason, tool path, workload, and version behind it; teams repeat failures or exclude viable regions. |
: **Every artifact exposes some design properties while leaving others to additional sources and checks.** Format selection affects which legal designs are easy, difficult, or impossible to express and which properties require information beyond that format. {#tbl-representation-formats tbl-colwidths="[22,34,44]"}

Two rows carry most of the argument.
